blurb: The Quebec heirloom 'Snow apple' — dark-red fruit with snow-white, tender, aromatic flesh that eats sweet-mild, not sharp. A beloved dessert and cider apple, but tender flesh, mild acid and a short storage life mean it misses the tart-crisp-keeper brief.
spread: Clumping — single grafted tree; needs a pollinizer apple nearby
seasons: White-pink blossom mid-spring; dark-red fruit Sept–Oct, eaten by midwinter
toxic: Fruit flesh edible; seeds contain cyanogenic amygdalin (mildly toxic if chewed in quantity)
origin: Central Asia and Afghanistan; cultivar a Quebec seedling of French stock, c. 1700
habitat: Wild fruit-tree forests and mountain slopes of Central Asia
gaps: No open-licensed photograph of the 'Fameuse' cultivar on the tree exists (the one Commons on-tree shot is OGL-licensed and 640 px; the CC Flickr hits are market bowls, book plates and text-overlaid frames), so the whole reel is honestly-captioned species-representative Malus domestica — red-fruited apples, blossom, foliage, habit and a winter shot.

care.hardiness: 'Fameuse' is one of the oldest apples in North America — first recorded around 1700 and reported in Quebec by 1730, either raised there from seed the French settlers brought or a French variety outright (the record does not settle which).[7][8] It was the most commonly grown apple in Quebec for over a century and a major commercial variety in the Champlain and St. Lawrence valleys, and is described as a very hardy tree — cold is no issue at all in Boulder's 5b–6a.[6][8] PlantTalk Colorado lists Fameuse by name among the apple varieties that are reliable in Colorado.[2] The genuine local risks are late-spring frost on the mid-season bloom and a wet spring bringing scab, not winter cold.[2][7]
care.planting: Plant in spring (April–May) or early fall, in full sun on well-drained, elevated ground rather than a low frost pocket, and not against a south or west wall — a warm wall pushes apples into bloom too early, where a Front-Range frost takes the crop.[2] Set bare-root trees while dormant, container stock through the growing season. In a pot the roots freeze far harder than ground roots over a Front-Range winter, so use a large (≥20 gal) container in a sheltered spot out of the wind (or an unheated garage in a hard cold snap) and plan to plant it in the ground within a year or two; the tree needs a steady inch of water a week from May through October, which a pot cannot hold.[3]
care.sun: Full sun, 6+ hours minimum and ideally all day; apples take partial shade but fruit, colour and disease resistance all drop as light does, and PlantTalk's Colorado guidance is full sun on an elevated, well-drained site.[2][4]
care.soil: Well-drained soil; the species tolerates clay, loam and sand across a broad pH from neutral into alkaline (>8.0), so Boulder's alkaline clay-loam is workable, happiest near 6.0–7.0.[4] Beach recorded that Fameuse did best on light, well-drained soil over a clay subsoil, and the nursery label's warning that it dislikes heavy soil agrees — amend heavy clay with organic matter at planting, plant on a slight mound, and never where water stands.[2][6]
care.water: Moderate, regular water — about an inch a week from rain or irrigation from May through October, applied as a deep soak at the dripline rather than frequent sprinkles, and never chronic wet feet.[3] Keep it even while the fruit is sizing in late summer; this tender-fleshed apple shows drought stress and irregular watering as small, soft fruit.[3][7]
care.spacing: Spacing follows the rootstock: roughly 6–8 ft for dwarf, 12–15 ft for semi-dwarf, and 20–25 ft for standard trees.[3] Fameuse is a vigorous, upright tree with sturdy long branches, so a semi-dwarf rootstock gives the most manageable backyard tree at about 12–15 ft, with the pollinizer it needs within 100 ft.[3][7]
care.propagation: Apples don't come true from seed, so 'Fameuse' is propagated only by grafting or budding a scion of the cultivar onto a selected rootstock — never from its own seed.[4] (Its own seedlings are famous for a different reason: McIntosh and Cortland are widely held to descend from it.)[7][9] The rootstock sets mature size, vigor and how soon it bears, so buy a grafted tree on a rootstock sized to your space.[3][4]
care.bloom: White-and-pink blossom opens in mid-spring, around May here — a mid-season bloomer.[2][7] Like all apples, 'Fameuse' is not self-fruitful and needs pollen from a different, co-blooming apple or flowering crabapple within about 100 ft — plant a compatible second variety to set a crop.[2][3] Because it flowers mid-season rather than late, a Front-Range frost after bloom can still take the crop; the elevated, non-south-wall siting matters.[2]
care.feeding: Feed lightly — nitrogen is normally the only nutrient apples need annually, and compost supplies it.[3] Keep nitrogen modest: heavy feeding pushes soft growth that delays bearing and invites fire blight, which strikes in warm, wet bloom-time weather here.[1][3]
care.pruning: Do the main structural pruning while fully dormant in early March, training to a central leader — one dominant trunk with tiered scaffold branches — and thinning crowded, crossing and inward wood to open the canopy for light and air, which also cuts the leaf-wetness that scab needs.[2][3] Fameuse is a vigorous upright grower, so annual pruning keeps it in bounds.[7] Fire blight is the Front-Range apple disease, so prune only in dry weather, disinfect tools between cuts, and cut out any blight strikes well below the visibly dead tissue.[1][2]
care.maintenance: Thin the fruit hard when it is marble-size in late June or early July — one or two per cluster, 4–6 in apart — both for size and to stop this heavy-bearing tree from settling into the crop-every-other-year rhythm the nursery label warns of.[3][8] Rake up and remove fallen leaves and fruit every autumn: scab overwinters in the leaf litter, and Fameuse is a scab-susceptible variety.[3][7] Dormant oil in late March covers scale, mites and aphids.[2]
care.troubles: Scab is the signature trouble — Beach noted the fruit is 'often badly injured by the apple-scab fungus', and Montana State rates it susceptible; a wet Front-Range spring is exactly when it hits, so the dry-climate advantage is real but not a guarantee.[6][7] Leaf-litter sanitation and an open canopy are the first line, with a preventive fungicide programme through the wet weeks of spring if the fruit has scabbed in prior years.[3][6] Fire blight is the big local disease of pome fruit — watch warm, wet bloom-time weather, keep nitrogen modest and cut out strikes in dry weather.[1] Codling moth is the most serious pest of pome fruits here and needs timed control after bloom for clean fruit.[1][2]
care.harvest: Pick in September into early October here — a late harvest on the Montana State scale — when the skin has deepened from bright red to near-purple-black over the shaded green-yellow ground.[7] Eat it soon. The flesh is snow-white (often streaked crimson under the skin), very tender and juicy, subacid becoming very mild subacid or sweetish, and aromatic — a spicy, distinctive dessert apple, not a sharp one and not a crunchy one.[6][7][8] Beach rated it decidedly inferior to other apples of its season for cooking, and storage is poor: it holds until about Christmas under good conditions, keeps best in a refrigerator at 33–38°F, and softens rather than staying crisp.[3][6][7]
care.companions: Plant a different apple variety or a compatible flowering crabapple within ~100 ft as the required pollinizer.[2][3] Keep the root zone in mulch or low groundcover rather than competing turf, and keep it away from junipers and hawthorns that host shared diseases.[1]

edible.card: Tender, snow-white, sweet-mild fruit — fresh or cider; short keeper
edible.summary: The fruit is a classic dessert and cider apple — snow-white, tender, aromatic flesh that eats mild-subacid to sweetish — best fresh within weeks of picking; only the seeds carry a trace toxin.[5][6]
edible.parts: The fruit (flesh and skin) is the edible part, fresh or cooked.[4] 'Fameuse' is prized above all as a dessert apple: Beach called it 'one of the most desirable dessert apples of its season', with flesh that is white, very tender, juicy, subacid becoming very mild subacid or sweetish, and aromatic.[6] That is the honest texture-and-flavor verdict — it is sweet-leaning with soft acid, and the flesh is tender rather than crisp, so it is not the tart-crunchy apple a crisp-keeper shopper is after.[6][7] It is also the traditional Quebec cider apple and cooks acceptably, though Beach rated it decidedly inferior to its season-mates for culinary use.[6][7]
edible.preparation: Eat fresh, ideally within a few weeks of picking — storage is poor, holding only until about Christmas under good conditions — or press for cider.[3][7] Core and slice for sauce if cooking; the flesh needs no special treatment to be safe, just discard the seedy core.[5]
edible.caution: The flesh and skin are entirely safe; the only concern is the seeds, which contain cyanogenic amygdalin like all apple pips. Amygdalin releases hydrogen cyanide only when seeds are crushed or chewed — whole seeds swallowed by accident pass through harmlessly, and it would take deliberately chewing on the order of dozens to hundreds of seeds to risk poisoning — so just core the apple, don't eat or grind the pips, and keep children and pets from chewing them.[5]
